tasks.short: Find the biggest losses, gather ideas from operators, work out improvements with engineering, get approval, implement and track them.

steps.what: Supervisor adds up downtime, scrap and speed losses from shift reports in a spreadsheet
Supervisor collects improvement ideas from operators on the floor and in team huddles
Supervisor works out better production methods with engineering and maintenance
Supervisor writes the proposal with costs and expected gains
Plant manager approves measures that need budget
Supervisor implements the change and coaches the team on the new method
Supervisor tracks actions and results on the paper improvement board

tasks.design: A loss Pareto in {BI}, built from machine stops, scrap and speed per line, replaces hand tallies; an improvement board in the {WORKFLOW} tool holds each idea with owner, status and before-and-after charts from the same data. Losses are shown per machine and line, never per operator, and the conversations and coaching stay with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Loss data came from paper shift reports and was added up by hand, so improvements were chosen on gut feeling.
tasks.enabler_now: Production monitoring tools collect stops and counts per machine and replace paper reports.
tasks.still_hard: Motivating people and changing habits is face-to-face work; downtime reasons are only as good as operators' entries.
tasks.human_edge: Getting operators to own the improvement and keeping it alive after the first weeks.

ambition.what: Improvements chosen each week from the top three losses, not once a year in a project.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor spends time on people and methods instead of tallying losses; budget decisions stay with the plant manager.

reach.learn: Whether the shared Pareto aligns engineering and floor priorities.

evidence.claim: A production monitoring tool replaced paper reports and spreadsheets at a building materials maker across 23 factories; no numbers given.
Systems that can observe operators' attendance or performance need works council consent.
AI that monitors and evaluates workers is high-risk; this design uses no model on people.

assumptions: Boundary: from loss analysis to tracked results; capital projects are outside.
Input contract: stops, counts and scrap per machine from the monitoring feed set up for production reporting; downtime reasons entered by operators; fallback is shift report tallies.
Plant manager time is outside the supervisor's savings.
Idea gathering, method work and coaching do not change.
unknowns: Whether downtime reasons are recorded per machine.
How many improvements per quarter the team runs.
research_questions: Does a weekly loss Pareto raise the number of improvements that last three months?

incremental.description: Supervisor checks downtime reason quality with operators.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: operators often skip downtime reasons, so the Pareto is not trusted and tallies return (9.5); high: reasons entered on most stops (15.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect counts, scrap and hours, reconcile with the ERP, work out unit costs and prepare the weekly management report.

steps.what: Operators book counts at manual stations and order hours at terminals
Supervisor types production counts and scrap from shift sheets into the spreadsheet
Supervisor enters labour hours per order from time bookings

Supervisor reconciles counts with production orders and fixes differences: by hand in the ERP today; after the change confirmations are prepared from counts and bookings and the supervisor resolves only differences
Supervisor checks the day's order confirmations: quantities, scrap and hours per order against the shift
Supervisor releases the checked confirmations to the ERP
Supervisor works out cost per unit from hours, scrap and materials
Supervisor prepares management reports of production results with charts and comments
Supervisor checks the final weekly report: figures against the week's confirmations and the comment against what happened
Supervisor sends the checked report to the plant manager: by e-mail today, released in {BI} after the change
Plant manager reviews the report and asks questions

tasks.design: Machine counts and operator entries at manual stations flow into the {OPS_SYSTEM}, order hours come from bookings in the time and attendance system ({OTHER}), and both prepare the production order confirmations, leaving only differences for the supervisor, who checks the day's confirmations and releases them once to the {ERP}. Unit cost is computed from the controller's rates, and the weekly report is generated in {BI}; the supervisor adds a short comment, checks the report and releases it once to the plant manager.
tasks.previous_blocker: Counts, hours and costs were re-typed from paper into spreadsheets because systems were not linked.
tasks.enabler_now: Production monitoring replaces paper reports, and time systems and ERPs exchange bookings as standard integration.
tasks.still_hard: Manual stations still depend on operators entering counts; hour bookings per operator need works council consent.
tasks.human_edge: Explaining to management what really happened behind the numbers.

ambition.what: Production results and unit costs available daily instead of a week later.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor checks differences and comments instead of compiling; decisions stay with the plant manager.

reach.task: Close production costs at month end
reach.learn: Whether daily confirmed orders shorten the close.

evidence.claim: A production monitoring tool replaced paper reports and spreadsheets across 23 factories in four countries; no numbers given.
Time systems and ERPs can exchange order hour bookings as standard integration.
Systems that can observe attendance or performance, and rules on staff personal data, need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from shift data to the report reviewed; month-end closing is outside.

Input contract: machine counts from counters connected by maintenance; counts at manual stations and order hour bookings entered by operators at terminals; cost rates set by the cost controller; fallback is the spreadsheet.
Hours are reported per order and line, not per operator.

Plant manager and operator time is outside the supervisor's savings; the operators' bookings are step s0 (share 1, other role). Both checks and the ERP release keep their full time; s6 keeps 20 for the release.

Coverage for s1 and s2: about 70% of output comes from machines with connected counters and the rest from operator entries at terminals; orders without bookings show as differences that the supervisor resolves.
unknowns: Share of output from manual stations.
Whether operators book hours on orders today.
research_questions: How many order confirmation differences remain each week after automation?

already_counted.description: Supervisor checks counts flagged as unusual.
Supervisor checks hour bookings flagged as missing or odd.
Supervisor reviews the generated report before release.

incremental.description: Cost controller keeps cost rates current.

approvals.approved_version: The week's report with figures and comment exactly as checked by the supervisor in s5c, released once in {BI} to the plant manager; changes after release need a new check.
The day's production order confirmations with quantities, scrap and hours exactly as checked by the supervisor in s3c, posted once to the {ERP} for those orders; any correction needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly manual stations and few order hour bookings, so much of the typing stays (51.4); high: about 70% of output from connected counters (70.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Spot shortages, requisition materials and supplies, chase delivery, request repairs and check what arrives.

steps.what: Operators scan empty kanban bins at the lines
Supervisor checks stock of consumables and supplies at the lines
Supervisor fills in a requisition with article numbers and quantities: on paper today, as a form in the procurement system for non-catalogue items after the change
Supervisor checks the final requisition: articles, quantities, the line and the need
Supervisor submits the checked requisition in the procurement system
Plant manager approves requisitions above the spending limit
Buyer checks the final order: lines, quantities, supplier and price against the requisition or bin scan
Buyer orders from the supplier
Supervisor chases purchasing by phone and e-mail about delivery dates
Supervisor writes the repair request for an equipment failure: by phone to maintenance today, in the maintenance management system with machine number and photo after the change
Supervisor checks the final repair request: machine, fault, photo and urgency
Supervisor submits the checked repair request to maintenance
Supervisor requests outside repair services when maintenance cannot fix the fault: by e-mail today, by a form in the procurement system after the change
Supervisor checks the service request: the fault, the service needed and the machine
Supervisor submits the checked service request to purchasing
Supervisor checks delivered materials and completed repairs

tasks.design: Consumables move to two-bin kanban: operators scan an empty bin and the {PROCUREMENT} system creates a requisition against a framework contract, which the buyer checks before ordering; the supervisor only requisitions non-catalogue items through a form there, checks each and submits it once. Order status is visible in the same system instead of by phone. The supervisor writes repair requests in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}) with machine number and photo, and requests for outside services in the procurement system, checking each before submitting it once.
tasks.previous_blocker: Requisitions were paper forms and status lived in the buyer's mailbox.
tasks.enabler_now: Purchasing systems support catalogues, framework contracts and kanban triggers, and maintenance systems take requests from a phone.
tasks.still_hard: Kanban only works if bins are scanned and min/max levels are right; urgent repairs still go by phone.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which shortage will stop the line tomorrow and pushing the right person.
tasks.altitude: The supervisor handles exceptions instead of filling forms; spending approval stays with the plant manager.

reach.learn: Whether photos and machine numbers shorten diagnosis.

evidence.claim: Purchasing systems support catalogues, framework contracts and kanban-triggered requisitions.
Maintenance management systems take repair requests with machine number and photo from a phone.

assumptions: Boundary: from spotting a need to checking what arrived; invoice matching is outside.

Input contract: min/max levels and framework articles set by purchasing; bins scanned empty by operators; machine numbers in the maintenance system kept by maintenance; fallback is the paper requisition.
Requisitions above the spending limit still go to the plant manager.

Buyer, plant manager and operator time is outside the supervisor's savings; the operators' bin scans are step s0 (share 1, other role). Writing repair requests, the checks and the submits keep their full time. s1 keeps 50 for line checks; s2 keeps 40 for non-catalogue items; s5 keeps 50 for chasing late orders; s7 keeps 80 because only the form layout changes.
unknowns: Share of supplies that can move to kanban.
Whether a maintenance management system is in use.
research_questions: Do line stoppages from missing supplies fall after kanban?

incremental.description: Supervisor checks that bins are scanned and levels fit use.
Purchasing keeps min/max levels and the catalogue current.

approvals.approved_version: The order lines exactly as checked by the buyer in s3b, after the plant manager's approval in s3 for lines above the spending limit, sent once to the framework supplier; changed lines need a new approval and check.
The requisition with articles and quantities exactly as checked by the supervisor in s2c, submitted once in the {PROCUREMENT} system; any change needs a new check.

The repair request with machine, fault, photo and urgency exactly as checked by the supervisor in s6c, submitted once to the maintenance queue in the maintenance management system; any change needs a new check.
The service request with fault, service and machine exactly as checked by the supervisor in s7c, submitted once to purchasing in the {PROCUREMENT} system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly non-catalogue parts and services, so most requisition work stays (16.2); high: consumables on kanban (27.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Request new hires, interview with HR, write and discuss evaluations, and propose promotions or contract extensions.

steps.what: Supervisor writes the request for a new hire: a vacancy form e-mailed today, a form in the HCM with the position data filled in after the change
Supervisor checks the vacancy request: position, hours, reason and start date
Supervisor submits the checked vacancy request to HR
Supervisor interviews candidates together with HR
Supervisor recommends the candidate to hire
Supervisor judges each operator's performance over the year
Supervisor writes annual evaluations for operators on paper forms
Supervisor holds the evaluation conversation with each operator
Supervisor writes proposals for promotions or contract extensions: by e-mail today, in an HCM form with the employee's data filled in after the change
Supervisor checks the proposal: the employee, the action proposed and the reasons
Supervisor submits the checked proposal to HR
HR advisor checks and processes the personnel action

tasks.design: Vacancy requests, promotion and extension proposals become forms in the {HCM} with position and employee data filled in; the supervisor writes the reasons, checks each and submits it once to HR. Evaluation forms in the {TALENT} system pre-fill last year's goals and completed training from the {LMS}; the supervisor writes every judgement, and no model scores or ranks operators.
tasks.previous_blocker: Forms were paper or e-mail attachments, retyped by HR.
tasks.enabler_now: HR systems offer request forms, evaluation forms and pre-fill from training records as configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Judging people fairly is the work; any model that evaluates workers would be high-risk and needs workers' representatives informed.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing each operator, giving honest feedback and backing the right people for promotion.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; less form work around each personnel action.

reach.learn: Whether routed forms cut back-and-forth with supervisors.

evidence.claim: AI that evaluates workers or decides on promotion is high-risk under the AI Act.
Workers' representatives must be informed before a high-risk AI system is used at work.
Rules on handling staff personal data need works council consent.
HR systems offer routed request forms and evaluation forms with pre-filled training records.

assumptions: Boundary: from requesting a hire or action to HR processing it; recruitment advertising and contracts are outside.
Input contract: employee data in the HCM kept by HR; goals entered in last year's evaluation; completed training from the learning system; fallback is paper forms.
HR time is outside the supervisor's savings.

Interviews, decisions, conversations, the checks and the submits keep their full time. s1 and s7 keep 80 because only position and employee data fill in and the supervisor writes the reasons; s5 keeps 80 because goals and training fill in and the supervisor writes every judgement.
unknowns: Number of operators the supervisor evaluates each year.
Whether evaluations are in an HR system today.
research_questions: Do routed forms shorten the time from proposal to processed promotion?

incremental.description: HR keeps forms and routing current.
No ongoing upkeep for the supervisor: learning the HR forms is a one-off, and using them is part of s1, s5 and s7.

approvals.approved_version: The vacancy request with position, hours, reason and start date exactly as checked by the supervisor in s1c, submitted once to HR in the {HCM}; any change needs a new check.
The proposal for that employee with the action and reasons exactly as checked by the supervisor in s7c, submitted once to HR in the {HCM}; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: employee data and last year's goals are often missing in the HR systems, so little fills in (2.2); high: data complete (5.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The production supervisor keeps people decisions, coaching and judgement; reports, requisitions and forms become generated or routed.
role.ambitious_version: A supervisor with daily results and costs who spends the week on improvements and people.

job.title: First-Line Supervisors of Production and Operating Workers
